proposals.relationship: Eldridge contrasts Cam’s legal and institutional interests with Power’s economic approach to medieval society.
proposals.evidence_note: Eldridge2021p174 explicitly sets Power’s choice of economic analysis apart from legal/manorial/constitutional topics pursued by her contemporaries and friends Cam AND AdaLevett;173–175 explains Power’s comparative sociology, literary vignettes and theoretical equipment. This is a bounded scholar-attributed contrast in research emphasis, not influence from friendship, identical women’s-history programmes, or a claim Cam lacked imagination/economic interests. Cam’s own selected1921administrative framing and1912comparative method establish her method’s breadth but are not fresh reading of Power originals. Levett missing endpoint; originalPower lecture/Berg biography unread.

proposals.relationship: Eldridge compares Cam and Hilton on how external demands could crystallize communal identity, while distinguishing Hilton’s Marxist emphasis on resistance.
proposals.evidence_note: Eldridge2021p190/n103 explicitly says Hilton’s class consciousness under central tax demands resembles Cam’s un-Marxist legal-historical work on communitas villae in external accounting, citing Hilton A Medieval Society1966p152 and Cam The Community of the Vill1950p1 (edsVeronicaRuffer/A.J.Taylor). Main text specifies resistance rather than cooperative sentiment in Hilton’s account and qualifies his view of law; these are Eldridge’s descriptions, not a demonstrated direct Hilton/Cam debate or every criticism silently assigned to Cam. Both cited original essays/books unread; undirected substantive comparison only.
